lede.text: Natural fibre and grass work gathers crafts of plant fibres: grass-based materials that are functionally similar but not taxonomically homogeneous, from bamboo and vetiver, which are grasses, to kora and kouna, which are sedges, rattan cane, a palm, and the screw pine, alongside coir from the coconut husk and bhimal bark fibre.

Some fibres are freed from husk or stem by retting in water, as with coir, jute and bhimal; bamboo and rattan cane are worked whole or split; and grass stalks and reeds are cleaved and woven round a base, as with sikki, coiled and woven, as with moonj, or woven on a loom, as with madur.

Its centres run from the coir of Kerala's saline backwaters and the madur mats of Purba and Paschim Medinipur to the sikki of Mithila, the kouna of Manipur and the bamboo crafts of North-East India, where approximately 66% of India's bamboo population is concentrated.

Women outnumber men in many grass-based craft traditions, especially screw pine weaving, moonj basketry is known for the large part rural women play in it and sikki art has proved a significant tool of women's empowerment in rural Mithila, while the Mahishyas of Medinipur weave madur mats, the Nath-Yogi of Sivasagar make bamboo gadgets and the Rudia of Uttarakhand make ringal articles.

sentences.text: In handicrafts, grass-based materials are a large group of plant fibres that are functionally similar but not taxonomically homogeneous.
Bast fibres come from plant stems and usually run their whole length, leaf fibres such as sisal are rough and sturdy, and coir comes from the fibrous husk of the coconut.
An account of cane and bamboo work around Allahabad distinguishes coiling for baskets from weaving for mats.
Bamboo has been used since time immemorial to craft utilitarian, decorative and even ritualistic objects, and it features dominantly in the craft traditions of many communities.

In North-East India different tribes and states make bamboo products from baskets, hats and flutes to bridges, houses and ropes, a craftsmanship that is widespread but not an exclusive occupation, and Arunachal Pradesh has a rich tradition of bamboo and cane handicrafts.
In Bengal madur is a generic word for floor mats, properly mats woven from a specific reed, and the madur kathi weavers of Medinipur are known as Mahishyas.
Moonj basketry in Uttar Pradesh is known for the large part rural women play in it, and most women Madhubani painters are also well versed in sikki art.
In Uttarakhand the makers of bamboo articles are called Baruree and the makers of ringal articles Rudia, both mainly highly marginalised scheduled caste families.

Plant fibre remains are rare in prehistoric South Asia; preserved jute fibres on a Harappan ceramic securely dated to 2200-1900 cal BC are the earliest evidence of jute textiles in the Indus civilization, and jute seeds from Rojdi in Gujarat date to approximately 2200-2000 BC.

The madur GI application traces mat weaving in India to the Indus Valley Civilisation and the Atharva Veda, and finds the first information about mat weaving in Bengal in records of the medieval period.

The madur GI application states that in 1744 a charter of Nawab Alibardi Khan made it obligatory for jaigirdars to supply masland mats for the collectorate, and that Kasijora and Narajol were then the two most important masland centres.
The same application cites a census report of 1872 that counted 618 skilled mat makers in Midnapore district, and reports that 448,300 mats were manufactured there in 1907-1908.

Fowler and Marsden derived the word coir from kayiru, rope, and wrote that coir fibre and rope went from India's West Coast to Europe from the middle of the fifteenth century, though coir articles were apparently not known in England until about the middle of the nineteenth.
Historically Sri Lanka was the largest exporter of coir fibre grades, while India focused on value-added coir products such as yarn, mats, ropes and rugs.

Kouna, closely associated with the tradition and culture of Manipur's Meitei community, was since time immemorial used only for making mats, and Pathamadai mats were mainly made by Labbai Muslim weaver families, a handwoven superfine silk mat being sent to Queen Elizabeth II for her coronation in June 1953.
The Ministry of Agriculture launched the National Bamboo Mission in 2006, and the Indian Forest (Amendment) Bill, 2017 removed bamboo from the definition of tree under the Indian Forest Act, 1927.
Bamboo belongs to the grass family, a hardy plant of many soils and climates, and an individual culm reaches its maximum diameter and height in a single spurt of growth, typically within 80-110 days.
Counts of bamboo differ: around 125 species in 23 genera in India by one count and 130 species in 18 genera by another, with about 19 genera and 78 species in North-East India.
In Uttarakhand ringal is a thin, spineless, reed-like bamboo of the mid and high hills above 2000 m, and dev-ringal, Himalayacalamus falconeri, is the ringal most used for articles.

Rattans are spiny climbing palms of the Old World tropics, around 600 species in 13 genera, of which Calamus, with about 370 species, ranges from the Indian subcontinent and south China eastward to Fiji.

Several materials are not grasses: kora is a sedge of the Cyperaceae, and kouna is two Cyperaceae club-rush species by one study, though Tata Trusts calls kauna a species of water reed, while rattan cane belongs to the palm family Arecaceae and screw pine to the Pandanaceae, and the madur reed of Medinipur is Cyperus tegetum or Cyperus pangorei.
Vetiver, Chrysopogon zizanioides, is a grass of the family Poaceae; sikki art of Mithila is made from its inflorescence stalks, while in South India art forms are made from its fragrant roots.
Moonj is the peeled outer layer of the thick green sarpat grass, a wild grass that grows richly near the river banks around Allahabad.

Coir is the fibrous mesocarp of the coconut, Cocos nucifera, bhimal, Grewia optiva, yields a strong bark fibre, jute fibre comes from highly lignified sclerenchyma cells in the phloem of its stems, and sisal, Agave sisalana, is a leaf fibre from leaves harvested yearly.
The husk makes up about 35% of a coconut's weight and about 30% of the husk is coir, while coir pith makes up 50 to 70% of the fibre.
Brown coir comes from mature coconuts and white coir from immature nuts, and retted white fibre is spun into yarn while brown fibre goes into rubberized coir and upholstery fittings.
Retted white coir has an average length of 35 cms and a diameter of 0.3 to 1.0 mm, and its stretch and resistance to decay in salt water suit it to floor coverings, cordage and marine work.
Cane is the rattan stem stripped of its leaf sheaths, solid, strong and uniform yet highly flexible, and among thirty-four Nath-Yogi bamboo gadgets cane completed the making of 27.

Bamboo comes naturally pre-finished with a smooth lustre, splits easily for weaving and has over 1,500 documented uses, and its culms attain full strength over 3-4 years after reaching full size, though the same manual elsewhere says bamboo takes 3-5 years to mature.
Borer beetles consume the starch in bamboo and bore tunnels along the culm that reduce its strength, while smoke from the hearth seasons lidded culm containers and protects them from insects.
About 20 percent of harvested rattan canes become stained, most commonly by blue stain fungi that penetrate deep inside the stem.
Kauna stems are soft, spongy, flexible and water-resistant, bhimal fibre is very long, fine and strong, and sikki items are almost immune to pest attacks.

Coconut husks are retted in the natural backwaters, in pits covered with soil and coconut leaves or in large nets called malis, for six to nine months, six to ten months, or ten months or even longer, as sources differ, and the loosened fibres were traditionally beaten out with wooden bars or mallets, a step since replaced by motorized steel drums with beater arms.

Jute stems, which generally take about 100 to 120 days to mature, are dried, defoliated and retted for 10-16 days in tanks or ditches with a reliable source of moving water, then decorticated by hand stripping, often by beating with a wooden mallet.

Inoculating husks with selected bacteria shortened retting by two and a half months in one field study and brought it down to three months in another, and the Central Coir Research Institute says its COIRRET consortium cuts retting from 11 months to 3 months.

Bamboo is crafted whole as natural hollow containers, as slats split along its length and as slivers woven into basketry, through stages from harvesting, cross-cutting and preservation treatment to radial splitting, sliver making and weaving.

Traditional bamboo preservation keeps felled culms in leaf to reduce their starch, soaks them so the starch leaches out, or treats them with castor oil and gentle heat or with smoke, protecting to a degree against borers but not totally against termites and fungus.

Rattan canes are used whole for furniture frames or split, peeled or cored for matting and basketry, and their primary processing includes deglazing, fumigation, bleaching and curing in a hot oil bath that turns the skin ivory white.

Sikki stalks are cleaved into as many as sixteen pieces and woven around a grassy base with a needle called takua, moonj coils are sun-dried and dipped in cold water before weaving, madur stalks yield 4 to 8 strips woven on a bamboo frame loom, and kauna is sun-dried and smoked before weaving.

Screw pine leaves are de-thorned, sun-dried and boiled in water with turmeric before weaving, the green cane of the muthra reed is soaked and sliced into thin strips for shital pati, bhimal fibre is retted in water bodies and beaten out, and the hemp fibre of the pula is plaited into ropes, twisted and stitched into the outsole.
Retting biologically degrades the polyphenols and pectins that hold coir fibres in the husk, while the lignocellulose of the fibre itself normally resists microbial attack.
Polyphenols leached from soaking husks inhibit the microorganisms responsible for retting, and a field study inoculated husks with phenol- and pectin-degrading Pseudomonas and Clostridium bacteria.
Yeasts play a vital role in degrading pectic and phenolic substances, and lime, sodium sulphate or sodium carbonate with hot water or steam can replace the microbiological process.

Fowler and Marsden traced the brown colour of fresh retting water to tannin extracted from the husk, the reddening of exposed fibre to tannin oxidising into phlobaphenes, and dull fibre to ferruginous floodwater forming tannate of iron.
Coir stands out for its high lignin content, reported at 37 to 42 wt% in one survey and about 31.9 wt% in another study, while bhimal fibre contains 14-16% lignin that is removed to make it flexible.

The bamboo cortex holds lignin and silica, bamboo is best harvested in the dry season when its starch content is lowest and starch-feeding borers and fungi attack less, and rattan's high starch content makes it liable to fungi and insects within one day of cutting.
A bamboo preservative is made as a 5% solution of boric acid and borax in the ratio 1: 1.5, and boron salts are effective against termites and fungi.
Sikki makers apply fast colours in hot water with common salt dissolved in it, and moonj dyers add salt to the boiling dye to help the colour last longer.
Coir has a helical cell wall with microfibrils at approximately 45 degrees, which explains its high resilience, and it stretches about 40% before breaking.
Sources differ on white and brown coir: one study cited in a review found white coir weaker, while Biswas and colleagues measured it slightly stronger, at 185 to 237 MPa against 165 to 222 MPa.

Bamboo fibres run longitudinally through the internode, which makes splitting easier, liquids travel quickly along the culm, and the modified Boucherie method forces preservative into fresh culms at between 1 and 1.4 kg/cm2.

Drinks keep fresh in culm containers whose outer skin is removed because the softer inner skin allows a limited degree of evaporation, and curing oil penetrates rattan cane along its axis but hardly through its skin.
Retting releases large amounts of phenolic compounds that give off a foul smell and affect aquatic flora and fauna, and temperature, water quality and tidal movement control how well husks ret.
Chemical extraction of bhimal fibre, such as urea retting, avoids the water pollution of the traditional retting method.
Bhimal and vetiver both check soil erosion with deep roots, bhimal on hill slopes and vetiver in flood-prone areas, where it is planted on field bunds against floods.

Rivers mostly emanating from the Nepal Himalayas leave much of Mithila waterlogged, a habitat for wetland grasses including Chrysopogon zizanioides, and frequent flooding around Midnapore makes the cultivation of madur grass an alternative for farmers.
Bamboo can be grown on degraded land, and cutting only mature culms keeps raw material available over a longer period without hampering the mother clump.
Trade has led to substantial over-exploitation of wild rattan, which with the loss of forest cover threatens the rattan industry, particularly in Southeast Asia.

Natural fibre products degrade at the end of their life, unlike synthetic alternatives, and most surveyed grass-based craft units in Kerala extract raw material directly from the forest, as do nearly 93% of surveyed ringal artisans in Uttarakhand.
Water hyacinth, Eichhornia crassipes, is an invasive aquatic plant that clogs waterways and reduces biodiversity in India's freshwater ecosystems.
Kerala's saline backwaters on the south-west coast provide natural facilities for retting coconut husks, which led to the coir industry, and Alappuzha dominates Kerala's coir sector.
Along the Malabar Coast retting relied on a tidal rise and fall of about 4 feet in the backwaters, and Fowler and Marsden placed the best coir on the West Coast of India and in the Laccadive Islands.

Approximately 66% of India's bamboo population is concentrated in the North-East, bamboo is put at around 12.8% of India's forest cover citing Tewari (1992), and bamboos occur in most regions except the Rajasthan desert and the upper reaches of Kashmir.

Citing Bhuyan and colleagues (2007), the Arunachal study gives Arunachal Pradesh 7770 sq. km under bamboo cover, the richest bamboo resources in the country, and bamboo culm containers for water and food are especially common in the North East.

Kouna grows wild and cultivated in the Imphal Valley wetlands of Imphal East, Imphal West, Thoubal and Bishnupur districts of Manipur, and Wright and colleagues noted in 2012 that jute is grown extensively in India, especially along the Ganges.

The madurkathi GI lies mainly in Purba and Paschim Medinipur, and the vetiver hubs of Mithila include Raiyam and Rampur in Madhubani district, Sursand in Sitamarhi district and the Tharuhat area of West Champaran.

Naini, a village by the Yamuna in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, is the major producer of moonj products, and Pattamadai mats of Tirunelveli district are produced from nanal, a natural straw growing on the banks of the Tamiraparani.
In Kerala, screw pine crafts are made mainly in Kottayam and Idukki, Palakkad and Wayanad make tribal crafts of bamboo, kora grass and reed bamboo, and Kasaragod focuses on cane craft.
The non-conducting property and sweat absorption of madur mats make them a household necessity in the hot and humid climate of West Bengal.
Coastal communities in Kerala developed treatments to make natural fibres resist humidity and a saline environment, especially in screw pine work.

Coconuts for retting were usually collected at about ten months old and pits set in the dry season rather than the rainy months of May to August, while sikki stalks are collected from the floodplains as the rainy season nears its end.

FAO estimated world coir production in 2019 at about 1.26 million tonnes, of which India produced almost half, 518,000 tonnes, and India's coir export earnings were approximately 130 crores of rupees in 1993-94.

A review citing Rethinam (2018) names China as the biggest coir export market, at 90% of export volume, and Fowler and Marsden wrote that coir soaking and separation appeared in general to be carried on as a cottage industry whose market value depended on the colour and fineness of the fibre.
Bamboo, known as the poor man's timber and the green gold of the forest, needs low initial investment, and the bamboo manual noted that many craftspersons used only a single tool, a dao or machete.

In a 2024 study, high-demand Nath-Yogi bamboo products earned craftsmen more per day than the average rural Indian worker, the murha, doon and khuka 78.57% more, while in a study published in 2011, 20% of surveyed ringal artisans in Uttarakhand earned Rs. 4000 to 6000 a month.
Sikki art has proved a significant tool of women's empowerment in rural Mithila, and in many grass-based crafts, especially screw pine weaving, women outnumber men in the workforce.

Tata Trusts reports that through a crafts programme it backs, women artisans in Thoubal district turned from kauna mats, which fetch little, to higher-value products, and in recent years kouna products have become a good source of income for many Meitei households.

Kerala's grass-based crafts face scarcer quality raw material and price competition from mass-produced plastic and synthetic goods, and the moonj article says exporters often take double what they give the worker.

In a 2025 study of a Meerut intervention turning water hyacinth into handicrafts, women artisans reported an average income rise of approximately 35%, and in July 2010 The Hindu reported pula pairs on sale in Himachal for as little as Rs. 60.
In vertical bamboo culm containers the nodal diaphragm forms the base, while horizontal containers keep both node walls intact to close the ends.

Designers and entrepreneurs, with traditional craft communities, are creating bamboo products for contemporary tastes, and kouna has diversified into handbags, coasters, hats, stools, cushions and chairs.
The japi of the Nath-Yogi is a rain shield of Himalayan fan palm leaves on an oval frame woven from thin bamboo strips, and their khuka fish trap holds fish behind two flexible inner openings.

Indigenous uses of rattan cane range from bridges and baskets to fish traps, furniture, crossbow strings and yam ties, and Chettinad kottans, traditional palm leaf baskets, were granted GI registration.
Madur weavers make three types of mat, the thin and light ak rokha, the heavier dui rokha and masland, the finest and most expensive.

Sikki gadgets are mostly containers for household and marital items, some with plant motifs such as the fruit of Trapa natans, and Rachna Sikki Hastakala Kendra, started in 1994, devised wall hangings of bent and pasted stalks.
Women of Allahabad and Gorakhpur make geometrical figures on circular moonj baskets, while the motifs of Tharu weavers are more animal-like.

The pula, in a way the state shoe of Himachal Pradesh, particularly of Kullu district, pairs an embroidered upper with a hemp fibre outsole, and agencies in Kerala have experimented with slippers and sandals of banana, arecanut and vetiver fibre.
Chemical bamboo preservatives range from relatively harmless boron salts, recommended for food-storage products, to toxic arsenic and chrome mixtures that need very careful handling.
Copper chrome arsenic is one of the most effective treatments for bamboo but is highly toxic, the use of arsenic is banned in some countries, and it is not suitable for products in contact with food.
People treating bamboo with chemical preservatives are told to wear gloves, face masks, eyeglasses and aprons and to keep children out of the treatment area.
